talk: Not every marketing channel wins fans at the same price. Work out the cost to win a fan on each channel, and how many months each fan takes to pay that back. Then move money to the channel that pays back fastest.

terms.meaning: Where a customer came from: social ads, radio, a school visit.
Customer acquisition cost. Spend on a channel divided by the customers it brings.
Cost to win a customer divided by the monthly profit they bring.

questions.prompt: Last season, social ads cost $30,000 and won 300 season ticket holders. Radio cost $40,000 and won 200. What did it cost to win a fan on radio?
questions.hint: Radio spend divided by radio fans.
working: Social: $30,000 / 300 = $100 per fan, half the price.
whyNot: $100 is the cost on social ads. Radio cost more and won fewer fans.
($30,000 + $40,000) / (300 + 200) = $140 is the average across both channels. The question is radio on its own.

questions.prompt: Each season ticket holder makes $20 profit a month. How many months does a radio fan take to pay back?
questions.hint: Cost to win divided by monthly profit.
whyNot: $100 / $20 = 5 months is social ads. Radio fans cost twice as much to win.
$140 / $20 = 7 months uses the average cost across both channels. Radio alone is $200.
20 x $10 = $200 assumes fans make $10 a month. They make $20, so it takes half as long.

questions.prompt: You move $30,000 from radio to social. Assume social keeps winning fans at $100 each. How many more fans do you get for the same money?
questions.hint: Fans on social minus the fans radio would have won.
working: 300 - 150 = 150 more fans for the same money.
Check the assumption: channels often get pricier as you spend more on them.
whyNot: Same money, but social wins fans at half the price, so you get more of them.
300 is all the social fans. Moving the money also means losing the 150 radio would have won.
300 + 150 = 450 counts the radio fans too. That money has moved, so radio wins nobody now.

penalty.prompt: You move {money} from radio, where a fan costs {radio} to win, to social ads, where a fan costs {social}. How many more fans do you get for the same money?
penalty.hint: Fans on social, minus the fans radio would have won.
working: {money / social|int} - {money / radio|int} = {money / social - money / radio|int} more fans.

traps.why: That's all the social fans. You also lose the ones radio would have won.
That counts the radio fans too. That money has moved.

call.title: Next season's marketing
call.prompt: You have $60,000. Social ads win fans at $100 each. Radio wins them at $200. A stadium tour day wins them at $60, but can only bring 200 fans.

options.label: All on social
options.result: $60,000 / $100 = 600 fans. Good, but the cheapest channel went unused.

options.label: Tour day first, the rest on social
options.result: Good call. 200 x $60 = $12,000 for the tour day. $60,000 - $12,000 = $48,000 left, and $48,000 / $100 = 480 fans. 200 + 480 = 680 fans. Fill the cheapest channel first.

takeaway: Compare channels on cost per fan and months to pay back. Move money to the fastest.
